papers.title: Where Rounding Happens Matters: Rounding-Location Alignment Stabilizes LLM Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Yijing Ke, Tianle Cai, Ruosong Wang
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning for large language models often uses separate systems for inference and training. Even with identical weights and BF16 tensors, implementation differences can make an intended on-policy update off-policy and destabilize training. Existing remedies align the entire inference and training stacks, change global precision, or modify the learning algorithm. We ask whether aligning selected parts of the execution stack can stabilize BF16 RL while other implementation differences remain. We align training-side rounding locations with inference in three regions---RoPE, SwiGLU, and residual RMSNorm---by retaining selected intermediates in FP32 until their BF16 outputs. Across four Qwen-family models, aligning all three regions prevents the collapse observed under the default BF16 baseline; RoPE-path alignment alone also suffices in the studied runs, despite remaining numerical discrepancies. The interventions keep the inference engine, matrix-multiplication and attention kernels, and learning objective unchanged.
papers.summary: LLM reinforcement learning usually generates answers with one inference engine and trains with another framework. Even with identical weights and BF16 on both sides, the numbers differ slightly, so an update meant to be on-policy quietly becomes off-policy and training can suddenly collapse. This paper from ByteDance Seed and Peking University finds that the two systems need not be aligned wholesale. It is enough to round at the same place on both sides in three spots, RoPE, SwiGLU and residual RMSNorm, keeping those intermediates in FP32 until their BF16 outputs. ==With all three aligned, four Qwen-family models no longer collapse==, and aligning RoPE alone also suffices. The inference engine, matmul and attention kernels, and the training objective stay unchanged.

papers.title: C 2 KV: Compressed and Composable KV Cache Reuse for Efficient LLM Inference
papers.authors: Chuheng Du, Junyi Chen, Hanlin Tang, Kan Liu, Tao Lan
papers.abstract: Long-context inference is central to modern large language model (LLM) applications such as retrieval-augmented generation. To mitigate the growing inference cost, recent work has explored non-prefix key-value (KV) cache reuse to reduce redundant prefill computation. However, existing reuse methods primarily focus on computation savings and overlook a critical bottleneck in long-context LLM serving: the cost of storing and accessing large KV caches. While KV compression appears to be a natural complement, naively combining compression with non-prefix KV reuse often leads to severe accuracy degradation. In this work, we propose C2KV, a unified framework for non-prefix KV reuse that jointly optimizes KV cache compression and concatenation. C2KV learns a composable and compressed KV cache manifold that is explicitly designed to be position-agnostic. Our approach introduces a lightweight sidecar Extractor with learnable compression tokens and a structured attention flow, enabling modular K
papers.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation stitches several retrieved documents into the context, and recomputing their KV caches from scratch every time is expensive, so some methods store each document's KV cache and concatenate them on use. But long documents have huge KV caches, so storing and loading them becomes the bottleneck, and naively compressing them before concatenation hurts accuracy badly. This paper from Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Alibaba proposes C2KV: a light extractor beside the frozen model reads each document followed by a few learnable compression tokens and keeps only those tokens' KV as the document's cache. ==Caches are stored without positions, which are re-applied at concatenation time==, so they combine like building blocks. On long contexts, inference is up to 17 times faster with generation quality largely preserved.

papers.title: Qdrant 1.20 - Full-Text Search Improvements
papers.abstract:
Qdrant 1.20.0 is out! Let’s look at the main features for this version:

BM25 on Full-Text Indexes and Code Search: Rank by BM25 straight from your payload text, with no embeddings to generate. Plus, better code search with a new code tokenizer.

Faster Nested Filters: A new per-element payload index answers nested filters without reading payloads, making them faster.

16-Bit and 8-Bit TurboQuant: A 16-bit TurboQuant datatype that halves vector storage without accuracy loss, and an 8-bit TurboQuant datatype and quantization option with recall close to float16.
papers.summary: Ranking keyword search results with BM25 in Qdrant used to mean turning every document and query into a sparse vector and tracking the average document length yourself, which drifts as data changes. Qdrant 1.20 computes BM25 directly on the full-text index: ==all statistics come from the data automatically, with no vectors to generate==. Parameters can be tuned per query, and it combines with vector search in hybrid queries. The release also adds a code tokenizer, so getUserName and get_user_name match each other, and a 16-bit TurboQuant vector format that halves storage versus the default 32-bit floats, with recall nearly unchanged on 12 datasets.

papers.title: NgramRL: Accelerating RL Post-Training for Structured Generation via Rollout-Aware N-gram Speculative Decoding
papers.authors: Nilesh Prasad Pandey, Jangseon Park, Jason Kong, Onat Gungor, Tajana Rosing
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but its cost is dominated by autoregressive rollout generation, which can exceed 70% of training time. Existing speculative-decoding methods are poorly suited to this setting: model-based drafters consume scarce GPU memory and may become misaligned as the policy evolves, while existing model-free methods do not explicitly exploit repetition across training epochs. We observe that recent rollouts of the same prompt provide a high-quality, self-updating draft source. Based on this insight, we propose NgramRL, a per-prompt n-gram drafter constructed from bounded recent rollout history. NgramRL requires no auxiliary model, drafter training, or persistent GPU-resident drafter state, while target-model verification preserves the rollout distribution. To hide CPU cache lookup and scheduling, we further introduce an adaptive fan-out prefetcher that predicts likely verification outcomes (j, b), consisting of the accepted draft length j and target-emitted continuation token b. A causal budget allocator concentrates prefetches on high-probability outcomes, while uncovered outcomes fall back to sequential lookup without changing committed tokens. Across two model families and three reasoning and structured-generation workloads, NgramRL commits 3.60-7.77 tokens per target-model forward in the warm-cache regime, up to 1.99x more than SuffixDecoding and 7.0x more than prompt-lookup decoding. On Spider, the prefetcher covers 96.6% of Qwen3-8B outcomes at a candidate budget of 16 and improves measured rollout throughput by 1.38x over synchronous NgramRL, approaching its 1.40x overlap ceiling.
papers.summary: In LLM reinforcement learning post-training, generating answers often takes over 70% of training time. This paper notices that the answers a prompt received in recent training rounds closely resemble what it will produce now, so they make good drafts. NgramRL ==builds an n-gram draft table for each prompt from only its own recent answers==. During generation, the last few tokens of the current answer are looked up in the table, what followed them becomes the draft, and the large model verifies several tokens at once. It needs no extra draft model and no GPU memory, and the output distribution stays the same. On reasoning and structured-generation tasks with a warm cache, each forward pass of the large model confirms 3.6 to 7.8 tokens, up to twice as many as SuffixDecoding, a similar method that drafts from a suffix tree over global past answers.

papers.title: KnitTrans: Coordinated Trajectory Transfer for Effective and Efficient LLM Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Bangjun Xiao, Chiheng Lou, Xiaodong Ji, Xiangwei Deng, Yikai Zhao, Gang Huang, Hailin Zhang
papers.abstract: Trajectory transfer from rollout to training affects both learning quality and system efficiency in large language model reinforcement learning (RL). Enforcing batch-wide training requirements can delay the admission of completed trajectories, resulting in higher architectural staleness: the additional parameter-version gap from disaggregated pipelining relative to colocated execution. Beyond admission, misalignment between data access and training consumption causes redundant movement and unnecessary waiting when transferring large trajectory payloads. We present KnitTrans, a system that coordinates the rollout-to-training path through three designs. First, constraint-preserving mini-batch admission allows flexibility in early mini-batch composition, while checking that enough capacity remains to satisfy the remaining quotas. Second, on-demand trajectory data access matches storage units to consumer assignments and overlaps micro-batch data preparation with computation. Third, multimodal encoding deduplication supports reuse across a mini-batch while preserving gradient contributions from all backbone micro-batches. Experiments show up to 93% lower architectural staleness than with train-batch admission, narrowing the learning-quality gap between disaggregated execution and colocated execution. On multimodal workloads, KnitTrans reduces transfer latency by two orders of magnitude and achieves a speedup of up to 5.8 times in transfer plus training over the baseline.
papers.summary: When LLM reinforcement learning runs generation and training on separate machines, finished trajectories often wait until a whole batch is complete before training, so the trained model drifts further from the version that generated them. Trajectory data is large, and mismatches between how it is moved and how training reads it cause repeated transfers and idle waiting. KnitTrans ==admits finished trajectories into early mini-batches==. A full batch must mix data sources at set ratios, so each admission is checked to leave enough room to fill every source's share. It moves data on demand in the order training consumes it, Several trajectories from the same prompt share its images and other multimodal inputs, so each input is encoded once per mini-batch and reused across them. The version gap drops by up to 93%, and on multimodal workloads transfer plus training is up to 5.8 times faster.

papers.title: How NVIDIA Mission Control 2.5 Brings Autonomous Recovery to Kubernetes
papers.abstract: Training large-scale AI models on thousands of GPUs is a high-stakes operation where monitoring and automation must be built-in to optimize cluster resiliency...
papers.summary: Large training jobs that run across hundreds of nodes for days or weeks will eventually hit hardware faults, software errors and network timeouts, and manual recovery wastes a lot of compute. NVIDIA's cluster management software Mission Control extends its automatic recovery engine from Slurm to Kubernetes training jobs in version 2.5. ==It first classifies the failure from the job's context, then decides whether to retry the job or isolate the machine==. On a hardware fault, the job is restarted or rescheduled while the bad node is quarantined and diagnosed in parallel. Transient software errors only trigger a retry, without needless hardware repair. It can also spot degrading nodes early and pull them from scheduling before a job is hit.

papers.title: Aquavit: Ascending Quantization for Communication-Efficient Vast-Scale Distributed Training
papers.authors: Hong Huang, Jiaxun Ye, Jinhai Yang, Wenjiao Feng, Zonghang Li
papers.abstract: Training Large Foundation Models (LFMs), including Large Language Models and Vision-Language Models, on massive distributed GPU clusters is increasingly bottlenecked by communication overhead. While frameworks like ZeRO++ employ static quantization to reduce communication volume, they suffer from a rigid trade-off: aggressive low-bit quantization maximizes throughput but introduces a persistent noise floor that impedes late-stage convergence, whereas high-precision quantization preserves accuracy at the cost of diminished training efficiency. In this paper, we propose the Noise Equivalent Hypothesis (Neophyte): the noise inherent to the weight quantization process plays a role functionally analogous to the stochastic gradient variance present in standard SGD optimization. We theoretically prove that just as a decaying learning rate is essential for convergence, an ascending quantization schedule is necessary to maintain optimization stability while maximizing throughput. papers.summary: Training large models on huge GPU clusters is increasingly limited by communication. Frameworks like ZeRO++ compress traffic with a fixed quantization bit width: low bits give high throughput but leave a constant noise floor that hampers late-stage convergence, while high bits keep accuracy but slow training down. This paper hypothesizes that weight-quantization noise acts much like stochastic gradient noise. It proves that, just as the learning rate must decay for convergence, ==quantization precision must rise over training== to keep optimization stable while maximizing throughput. The resulting Aquavit quantizes communication with few bits early in training and switches to more bits later.

papers.title: Accordion: Elastic-Depth Inference via Fixed-Prefix Layer Looping
papers.authors: Yudong Zhang, Wei Ding, Kaili Zheng, Yuchen Ding, Zhenyu Zhang
papers.abstract: Large language models serve applications with diverse inference budgets, but training and maintaining separate models for each budget incurs substantial costs. Recent Looped Transformers enable flexible inference computation through parameter reuse, but maintaining strong performance across different inference budgets remains an open challenge. We introduce Accordion, a mixture-of-experts-based model that supports five inference budgets through fixed-prefix layer looping. Each budget follows a pre-defined execution path, while the minimum budget retains the unlooped model. Joint pretraining samples one budget per micro-batch and optimizes its next-token prediction loss without additional cross-budget consistency objectives. We further preserve these inference budgets through supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, where parameter-group merging and budget-matched multi-teacher on-policy distillation integrate three domain experts into one model. After 3.6T tokens of pretraining, increasing inference depth improves Accordion-6B-A0.5B's five-category macro-average across 37 tasks by 3.01 percentage points, with the middle budget capturing 89% of this gain using half as many additional layer executions. The final model surpasses each domain expert on its corresponding task-and-budget average, while achieving strong instruction-following performance across all budgets and retaining depth-dependent gains in mathematical reasoning and code generation.
papers.summary: Serving one large model under different inference budgets is costly if each budget needs its own trained and maintained model. Accordion is a mixture-of-experts model that serves five inference budgets with one set of weights. A run of middle layers forms a loop window; each budget runs the first few layers of that window twice in a row, higher budgets repeat more layers, and the lowest budget is the unlooped model. Pretraining samples one budget per micro-batch, with no extra consistency objective. ==The middle budget gets most of the top budget's gain at half the extra compute==. Deeper inference raises the average across 37 tasks by 3.01 points, and the middle budget captures 89% of that.

papers.title: Beyond Hotness: High-Resolution Memory Characterization of Cloud and LLM Workloads for Tiered Memory with ARM SPE
papers.abstract: Memory demands from data analytics and LLM workloads grow rapidly, driving up memory costs in cloud and data centers. Multi-tier memory has emerged as a promising solution to balance performance and cost. However, effectively leveraging it requires a deep understanding of workload memory behaviors. This work introduces a high-resolution memory characterization methodology for analyzing workload-specific opportunities for multi-tier memory usage. In response to the increasing deployment of ARM-based processors in data centers, we implement our methodology using the recent Statistical Profiling Extension (SPE) for ARM. By characterizing eight memory-intensive workloads from CloudSuite and LLM applications, we identify region-specific access patterns, evaluate the effectiveness of cloud-oriented cache hierarchies, and propose new metrics based on memory idle periods and latency profiles to determine suitable data placement for tiered memory.
papers.summary: Memory demand from data analytics and LLM applications is growing fast, so data centers are adopting tiered memory that puts cold data on cheaper, slower memory. But deciding which data goes to which tier by access hotness alone is often imprecise. This paper uses the Statistical Profiling Extension (SPE) on ARM processors for high-resolution memory profiling of eight memory-intensive cloud and LLM workloads. It splits memory into contiguous regions and builds each region's access-latency distribution: ==regions with long latencies deserve the fast tier==. It also measures each region's longest stretch without accesses; the longer it sits idle, the better it suits the slow tier. It also evaluates how well cloud-oriented cache hierarchies work.

papers.title: Tile-Based Decompression in Compiled GPU Engines
papers.authors: Antonio Boffa, Ananya Gupta, Hamish Nicholson, Anastasia Ailamaki
papers.abstract: Modern GPUs reach record analytical performance only when a query's working set fits within its GPU memory budget, and that budget is under growing pressure: GPUs are partitioned and shared, working sets are outgrowing high-bandwidth memory (HBM), and HBM is a fixed on-device resource whose per-dollar capacity has stagnated across generations. Lightweight compression can relieve this pressure by shrinking both footprint and bandwidth demand, but existing GPU compressed-execution techniques either bind decompression to a specific execution model or materialize decompressed columns in HBM before query execution. We present a compression subsystem for compiled GPU query engines that treats decompression as a first-class physical operator. Compression-specific logic is isolated behind a narrow backend interface, so new GPU-oriented encodings can be added without rewriting downstream operators. We implement the design in Proteus and study where decompressed values should be materialized in the GPU memory hierarchy. Our compiler-integrated shared-memory strategy fuses cooperative tile decompression with tuple-at-a-time query execution inside a single generated GPU kernel, avoiding decompressed-column materialization in HBM. Compared with HeavyDB and Sirius on GPU-resident data, fused on-chip decompression achieves competitive query times while reducing the resident memory footprint by up to 4x and memory-bandwidth consumption by up to 6x.
papers.summary: GPUs run analytical queries fast only when the data fits in GPU memory, which is shared among jobs and whose capacity per dollar has barely grown across generations. Compression saves memory and bandwidth, but existing approaches either tie decompression to one execution model or write decompressed columns back to GPU memory before the query runs. This paper makes decompression a standalone operator in the compiled GPU query engine Proteus: ==tiles are decompressed in on-chip shared memory and fused with the query in one GPU kernel==, so decompressed data never goes back to GPU memory. Against HeavyDB and Sirius, query times are comparable while resident memory drops by up to 4 times and bandwidth use by up to 6 times.
